results.title: When Copper Wire Meets Al-Fed Liquid Metal: A Visual Demonstration of Self-Sustained Oscillation
results.abstract: Abstract Oscillation is a fundamental dynamic phenomenon in nature and technology. We present a visually striking and easy-to-implement demonstration experiment suitable for senior undergraduates in physics, chemistry, or materials science. When a copper wire is inserted into a droplet of aluminum-fed gallium–indium liquid metal (LM) immersed in aqueous NaOH solution, the wire begins to oscillate spontaneously and periodically. The motion is driven by a feedback loop between the aluminum–hydroxide reaction, localized hydrogen evolution, and asymmetric capillary forces at the three-phase contact line. The experiment uses only common materials (Ga–In alloy, aluminum foil, copper wire, NaOH), requires no complex instrumentation, and can be completed in less than 30 min. Its vivid, self-sustained oscillation engages students and illustrates core concepts of surface tension, reactive wetting, and chemically induced motion. Detailed safety precautions and waste-disposal protocols are provided, along with open-source video and motion-analysis files to facilitate adoption in the classroom. The demonstration also opens discussions on dynamic systems and the design of soft actuators.

results.title: Active Oscillations of Elastic Membranes Arising from the Coupling with a Catalytic Reaction
results.abstract: Soft fluidic machines increasingly rely on self-sustained oscillations to accomplish tasks autonomously without electronics or software. Typically, these oscillations arise from mechanical nonlinearities in complex geometries or relatively involved fluidic circuitry, and are passive in that they require external power sources. Here, we show that, by harnessing the coupling with a catalytic reaction, active oscillations can arise even in flat elastic membranes without fluidic circuits or external power. We embed a silver catalyst in a flat elastic membrane suspended over a pool of liquid hydrogen peroxide as fuel. When the fuel contacts the catalyst, it decomposes, releasing gases and generating pressure. We observe an oscillation where the reaction activates and deactivates spontaneously, causing the membrane to cyclically inflate and deflate for hours consecutively. Using experiments and a lumped-parameter model, we show that the oscillation arises from an interplay between catalyst capillarity, membrane stiffness, and venting resistance, which together induce negative feedback and separation of timescales. These results demonstrate an active oscillation in which the energy release is directly coupled to the oscillation dynamics. By embodying energy within the oscillation, we expand the library of phenomena to achieve self-oscillation in autonomous soft machines, opening avenues for elasto-chemical strategies for physical control.

results.title: Diffraction, Talbot Oscillations and Fourier Optics in the Undergraduate Physics Laboratory
results.abstract: Abstract Diffraction experiments in the Fraunhofer and Fresnel regimes and their analysis using Fourier optics are discussed. The focus is on gratings, but to emphasize the mathematical details, results on single slits are also presented. Measurements in the Fraunhofer regime form the basis of this study. The Fresnel regime is explored by bringing the diffracting object and the camera closer together. The power of the Fourier analysis is particularly evident, when studying self-imaging via the Talbot effect and Talbot oscillations at gratings. Expressions are derived for the amplitude oscillations of Fourier space patterns, enabling the Talbot length to be determined precisely. These experiments are designed for use in second-year undergraduate general physics laboratories.

results.title: Spontaneous oscillations and geometric cutoff in confined bacterial swarms
results.abstract: Self-organized dynamic patterns in dense active matter are striking manifestations of non-equilibrium physics. A prominent example is the macroscopic elliptical motion observed in quasi-2D bacterial suspensions, which has lacked a physical explanation. Here, we examine a minimal linear response framework coupling bacterial swimming dynamics with fluid flow, treating long-range hydrodynamic interactions as a macroscopic communication channel. We demonstrate that microscopic swim motion, via Jeffery coupling, manifests as a ``phase-leading'' response to local shear flows. System-wide sustained oscillations, on the other hand, require both a critical bacterial density and strict geometric confinement. By analytically predicting the onset cell density and maximum film thickness, our model achieves excellent quantitative agreement with experiments, establishing a unified physical framework for self-organized periodic motion of elongated body in active fluids.

results.title: ELM-CLAIM: a claim-calibration framework for adaptive, memory-like, learning-like, and goal-directed claims in engineered living materials
results.abstract: Engineered Living Materials (ELMs) combine living cells with matrices, interfaces, environmental fields, and sometimes electronic or computational controllers. Their multicomponent architecture creates an attribution problem: the same observed output may reflect passive material physics, active cellular regulation, interface or morphological change, environmental gradients, controller adaptation, or coupled-system dynamics. This article proposes ELM-CLAIM (Engineered Living Materials-Controls for Learning, Adaptation, Intelligence, and Memory), an author-proposed claim-calibration and reporting framework for matching adaptive vocabulary to measurable state variables, temporal criteria, attribution targets, and evidence classes. The framework classifies specific behaviors from passive responsiveness (L0) through active responsiveness (L1), adaptation (L2), memory-like behavior (L3), learning-like behavior (L4), and autonomous goal-directedness (L5). It also provides an evidence-tiered claim-to-control matrix, proportional substitution rules for experimentally intractable controls, component- and controller-level attribution logic, model-transparency requirements, and a reviewer-oriented reporting checklist. Essential entries denote evidential functions rather than a single mandatory assay, allowing justified orthogonal controls while requiring claims to be lowered when major alternatives remain unresolved. Published cases are used illustratively to stress-test interpretability rather than to validate the framework statistically. ELM-CLAIM calibrates language; it does not by itself validate an experiment, define cognition, or constitute a community standard. Community testing, inter-reviewer reliability assessment, and prospective experimental use remain necessary next steps.

results.title: Assisted adaptation of kelps for a warmer ocean: Thermal priming and induction of memory stress in Macrocystis pyrifera and Eisenia arborea
results.abstract: Kelp forests are under increasing threat from ocean warming and marine heatwaves. In this context, assisted adaptation techniques emerge as promising tools for optimizing conservation and restoration strategies. One such technique is the cross-generational induction of stress memory by thermal priming, which aims to stimulate the thermal tolerance of kelps in the face of warming. However, research into these processes is still in its infancy. Here, we evaluated whether sublethal warming (priming) applied to gametophytes (23°C for 25 days) enhances the thermotolerance of the resulting juvenile sporophytes of Macrocystis pyrifera and Eisenia arborea. After the priming phase, we compared the biological performance of juvenile sporophytes derived from primed and non-primed gametophytes at two temperatures: a severe warming (25 °C for five days) that simulates regional marine heatwave conditions, and a control temperature of 17 °C. Under severe warming, sporophytes derived from non-primed gametophytes experienced complete mortality in both species, whereas sporophytes derived from primed gametophytes survived, maintained physiological function and grew. These sporophytes exhibited similar or even higher photosynthetic capacities than those at 17°C and did not show evidence of oxidative damage. Overall, these findings prove that applying thermal priming to gametophyte stage can increase thermotolerance in subsequent sporophyte generations, preventing mortality and improving physiological performance at temperatures that would otherwise be lethal. The present study provides initial evidence that the induction of cross-generational memory stress can be applied to M. pyrifera and E. arborea, paving the way for the development of future conservation and restoration strategies.

results.title: Memory and Technology: 4E Perspectives
LUMENRYX 5: Independent-State Optical Tensor Memory — A Post-Lithographic Architecture for 100-TB-to-Petabyte Executable AI Memory and ASI-Scale Computing
results.abstract: LUMENRYX 5 presents a complete research program for a radically different class of computing hardware: a post-lithographic optical computer in which extremely large AI models are retained directly as independently usable physical states and participate directly in computation. The central objective is to remove one of the fundamental constraints of contemporary AI hardware-the separation between processor, accelerator, memory, and model storage-and replace it with a unified executable optical memory substrate capable, in principle, of scaling from conventional AI systems toward hundreds of terabytes and ultimately petabytes of resident model state. Rather than treating optical storage as a passive archive, LUMENRYX develops Independent-State Optical Tensor Memory, in which persistent material states encode model coefficients and selected states directly contribute to optical tensor operations when illuminated. The intended long-term result is a computing medium in which the model does not need to be repeatedly fetched from HBM or transferred through a conventional GPU memory hierarchy: the stored physical state itself becomes part of the computational operator. The research develops this concept from first principles through a sequence of increasingly concrete architectures, culminating in a proposed sublattice-addressed fluorescent tensor-memory system designed to combine very high volumetric information density with selective optical execution. Hugging Face: PureOne/LUMENRYX-5-ASI-Optical-Tensor-Memory · Datasets at Hugging Face Major results and contributions include: A framework for persistent executable optical memory, separating long-term retained model state from transient optical energy. A constructive method for representing arbitrary signed low-bit tensor weights as independently stored physical states that directly participate in matrix-vector computation. A sublattice addressing architecture that allows extremely dense physical storage to coexist with a coarser optical addressing system. Quantitative design studies for 100 TB, 500 TB, and 1 PB of independently represented model information. A sufficient mathematical condition for genuinely independent programmability in the presence of nonlinear write cross-coupling, rather than equating nominal cell count with usable memory capacity. A photon-allocation optimization that reduces modeled detected signal-photon requirements by approximately 33.6% at fixed error in the studied case. Large-aperture execution analysis showing how increasing optical field width can reduce the number of parallel execution heads required for extremely large models. Calibration architectures whose metadata can scale with matrix dimensions rather than requiring an independent high-precision correction value for every stored coefficient. Arithmetic integrity checks for detecting and correcting selected classes of computational faults in an analog optical tensor substrate. A separation between a very large retained base model and smaller high-speed programmable regions for adaptation, model updates, fine-tuning, or future self-modifying AI systems. Explicit analyses of memory density, addressing, optical precision, photon statistics, storage utilization, write throughput, working memory, manufacturing throughput, access latency, and full-system energy. A staged physical validation protocol progressing from small signed fluorescent tensor operators to dense sublattice-addressed memories and eventually large resident-model systems. A complete consolidation of the preceding NOEMACRYST–ISOPHASE and LUMENRYX research sequence into a single reproducible public package. Under one declared high-density scenario—112 nm transverse cell pitch, 1 μm layer spacing, and 25% net usable memory fraction—the calculated assigned memory-region density is approximately 2.49 TB/cm³, corresponding to approximately: 40 cm³ for 100 TB 201 cm³ for 500 TB 401 cm³ for 1 PB These are conditional geometric design calculations rather than experimentally demonstrated memory capacities. The work explicitly distinguishes nominal physical density from independently programmable, reliably readable, computationally useful information. At four bits per parameter, 500 TB corresponds to approximately one quadrillion independently represented parameters, before redundancy, calibration, working memory, checkpointing, or other system overhead. This scale is relevant to investigating future AI architectures whose resident parameter capacity would be difficult to accommodate within conventional accelerator memory hierarchies. The long-term technological objective is a fluid, physically unified AI computing substrate that could reduce or eliminate repeated movement of enormous weight matrices between separate memory and compute devices. If the required material, optical-access, precision, manufacturing, and energy conditions can be satisfied experimentally, the architecture could enable systems with a very different scaling regime from contemporary CPU/GPU/HBM computing. Possible future implementations range from large ASI-oriented research systems to smaller AGI-class modules, workstation-scale AI computers, and eventually highly integrated consumer hardware. In the most mature form, such technology could move toward a computer in which persistent model memory, tensor execution, adaptation, and optical communication occupy one closely integrated physical platform rather than a conventional hierarchy of CPU, GPU, DRAM, HBM, storage, and interconnect. This potential is particularly significant for ASI-scale models, where resident model capacity, memory bandwidth, data movement, and energy consumption may become as important as raw arithmetic throughput. LUMENRYX therefore treats memory not as a peripheral component but as the central computational medium. The research does not claim that a petabyte executable optical computer, ASI system, or experimentally verified GPU replacement has already been built. Physical qualification remains outstanding. Instead, the release provides a detailed theoretical and computational architecture, identifies the critical experiments needed to falsify or validate it, and establishes quantitative requirements that a real implementation would need to satisfy. The complete release contains the full chronological research program, mathematical derivations, architecture specifications, numerical experiments, source code, automated tests, generated data, figures, machine-readable results, physical prototype protocols, failure analyses, scaling studies, and reproducibility material. The broader goal is to investigate whether AI hardware can move beyond decades of processor-centric architecture toward a new regime: model state as material state, memory as computation, and extremely large AI systems as resident physical structures rather than workloads continuously transported through conventional processors. If experimentally validated at scale, this approach could represent a path toward post-GPU, post-lithographic AI hardware with hundreds of terabytes to petabytes of directly usable model state, potentially enabling levels of model capacity and integration that are impractical with conventional accelerator-memory architectures. Research status: theoretical architecture, mathematical analysis, numerical validation, and prototype specification. Large-scale physical realization and GPU/ASI performance claims remain to be experimentally demonstrated. Made by Artificial Hyperintelligence Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki

results.title: Intrusive Memories
Educational Materials for Health-Related Discrete Choice Experiments: A Theory-Driven Approach
results.abstract: BACKGROUND: To make informed choices in health-related discrete choice experiments (DCEs), respondents need to understand the choice scenarios, alternatives, attributes and attribute levels presented to them. Respondent populations are often highly diverse in knowledge and experience, leading to varying informational needs that make it challenging to design educational materials that sufficiently inform all respondents without disengaging others. At present, however, structured guidance on developing DCE educational materials is lacking. Drawing on the instructional design literature, this paper investigates whether theory-driven adaptations to educational materials improve respondent comprehension and engagement in health-related DCEs. METHODS: Informed by three focus groups on DCE informational needs, we identified four design principles from the instructional design literature relevant to DCE educational materials: whole-task instruction, making inferences explicit, adapting information to respondents' prior knowledge and embedding self-check questions with corrective feedback. Educational materials for three existing DCEs (influenza vaccination, colorectal cancer screening and rheumatoid arthritis prevention) were redesigned to incorporate these principles. Panel respondents (N = 1754) were randomized to receive either the original or the adapted educational materials, and effects on comprehension, engagement, internal validity and choice consistency were assessed. RESULTS: Adapted materials increased time spent on educational content and were associated with small improvements in selected comprehension outcomes, though effects were often not statistically significant against the co-created comparator. Self-check questions revealed considerable comprehension gaps regardless of condition, underscoring that co-creation and pre-testing alone do not guarantee sufficient respondent comprehension. Educational materials also emerged as a meaningful source of selective dropout in all surveys, predominantly among respondents with lower education levels, posing a risk to sample representativeness that warrants attention in future research. DISCUSSION: Adapting DCE educational materials based on educational theory and instructional design principles offers a promising approach to improving respondent engagement and understanding. To enable cumulative learning, we further encourage researchers to report comprehension outcomes and publish educational materials as supplementary materials.

results.title: Self-disclosure as a distinctive correlate of collective prosocial behavior in youth organizations
results.abstract: Gotong royong is an important form of collective behavior in Indonesian youth organizations, yet the interpersonal factors associated with its development remain insufficiently examined. This study investigated the relationships of self-disclosure and resilience with gotong royong among members of Dewan Anak Mataram (DAM), a youth organization in Mataram, West Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia. A quantitative cross-sectional correlational-predictive design was employed. Participants were 47 active DAM members selected through total sampling. Data were collected using three 15-item four-point Likert scales measuring self-disclosure, resilience, and gotong royong. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, simple linear regression, and multiple linear regression. The findings showed that self-disclosure was positively correlated with gotong royong (r = .660, p < .001), as was resilience (r = .539, p < .001). When examined simultaneously, the two predictors explained 45.2% of the variance in gotong royong (R² = .452, adjusted R² = .427, F(2,44) = 18.169, p < .001). Self-disclosure showed a significant unique association with gotong royong (β = .543, p < .001), whereas resilience did not (β = .174, p = .254). These findings indicate that self-disclosure is a distinctive correlate of gotong royong within this organizational context, while the bivariate association between resilience and gotong royong largely overlaps with shared variance between the predictors. The findings highlight the relevance of constructive communication and interpersonal openness in understanding collective behavior among youth organization members.

results.title: Frequency heterogeneity can promote order yet undermine stability in Kuramoto networks with higher-order interactions
Postphenomenological Insights from an In-the-Wild Collective Sensing System Deployment for PTSD Therapy
results.abstract: Treatments like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) have high clinical efficacy for a variety of mental health disorders. Their effectiveness, however, is often limited by low patient engagement with clinical homework. Novel technologies are accordingly being integrated into clinical mental health workflows, but this is a delicate endeavor and studies of in-the-wild clinical deployments remain rare in the CSCW and HCI communities. Lab-based and theoretical design studies are valuable first steps toward integration, but they struggle to disambiguate the real-world impacts of novel technologies on ecologically sensitive clinical environments as the relationships between human actors and technologies are co-constituted. We developed a collective sensing system meant to help contextualize patient homework exercises within a two-week CBT intensive outpatient program (IOP) for PTSD. We then conducted an in-the-wild field deployment study involving 20 patients and 10 clinicians over 15 months. The system received strong performance ratings for usefulness, usability, and preliminary efficacy, and, in interviews, patients and clinicians reported that it facilitated collaborative clinical homework review and accountability throughout the therapy process. We also found four themes related to its unexpected real-world impacts on CBT practice surrounding emotional processing, patient agency, accountability, and contextual trust. Given the observed complexity of relationships developed between patients, clinicians, and the collective sensing system, we ultimately draw from the philosophical tradition of postphenomenology and conduct a “variational cross-examination” of our findings to discuss implications for future deployments. Our work highlights the importance of clinical deployments and the subsequent value of postphenomenological analysis to the CSCW and HCI communities.

results.title: Statistical mechanics of restroom choice
results.abstract: Human behavior is influenced not only by social interactions but also by the way people interact with their environment. Understanding these different interactions in constrained environments is a central question in behavioral science, but it remains challenging due to the difficulties of data collection. We focus on restrooms with a given number of sites, such as urinals or toilets, as a minimal setting for investigating human behavior. We introduce a web-based platform that enables the collection of large-scale data on sequential occupancy choices in controlled restroom layouts. We analyze transition probabilities between configurations using a statistical physics framework inspired by the Ising model, from which we infer effective interpersonal interactions and site-dependent biases. We further develop a kinetic model describing individual arrivals and departures, which allows us to predict site usage as a function of the utilization factor. Finally, we demonstrate that the model generalizes across restroom of different sizes, enabling prediction of usage and dynamics from limited data. Beyond this specific system, our results demonstrate how simple local rules can generate predictable collective behavior in constrained environments, with implications for a broad class of public spaces such as waiting room or public transportation.

results.title: Unexpected Extemporaneous Anomalous Reactions (UNEARs) and their Relationship with Meditation
results.abstract: The beneficial effects of meditation have attracted increasing scientific interest, particularly regarding the mechanisms through which this ancient practice may contribute to health recovery and maintenance. Nevertheless, despite the broad range of benefits attributed to meditative practices, the literature also reports numerous unusual experiences related to meditation. This study describes reports from three novice practitioners of meditation who experienced unexpected reactions, including headache, sudden sialorrhea, sudden heat in the body, drowsiness, feeling indisposed, an increase in anxiety and aggressiveness, jealousy, crying episodes, a desire to discontinue meditation practices, feeling faint, anguish, and fear of consciousness leaving the body, among others. These reactions are referred to here as “unexpected extemporaneous anomalous reactions” (UNEARs) — a phenomenon linked to the multidimensionality of the Being that may, in some cases, result from the confrontation between the practitioner and the Self shaped by an individual’s life experiences over time. With basis on qualitative data collected from semi-structured meditation diaries containing three open-ended questions that allowed practitioners to describe in detail any experienced reactions, and considering empirical observations of several dozen novice practitioners in previous meditation courses, the current study aims to propose an etiological hypothesis comprising three inducing factors that may act as “triggers” of UNEARs: (I) failures in the execution of the exercises, (II) the adaptation of the Being’s multidimensional body to meditation, and (III) the “unearthing effect” of meditation. These factors may contribute to the development of further rigorous investigations into the possible existence of a subtle human anatomy composed of chakra systems and nadis, as well as its relationship with anomalous experiences associated with certain holistic and alternative practices.

results.title: Electrohydrodynamic jet stability of ionic liquid–hydroxylammonium nitrate (HAN) mixtures under thermochemical propulsion constraints
results.abstract: Hybrid propulsion systems combining electric and chemical propulsion have attracted considerable attention because they can provide both high specific impulse and high thrust within a single propulsion architecture. This study investigates the feasibility of ionic liquid–hydroxylammonium nitrate (HAN) mixtures as a single propellant for hybrid electro-chemical propulsion systems through electrospray experiments and thermodynamic performance analysis. Electrospray experiments were conducted under atmospheric conditions using a downward-oriented annular slit emitter to examine the effects of HAN concentration, applied voltage, and flow rate on jet morphology, droplet formation, and pulsation behavior. Increasing HAN concentration significantly altered electrospray characteristics by reducing viscosity and increasing electrical conductivity. Higher applied voltages promoted finer atomization and increased pulsating frequency, whereas higher flow rates generated larger droplets due to enhanced inertial effects. Among the tested compositions, mixtures containing 50%–75% HAN exhibited stable jet emission, favorable atomization characteristics, and enhanced pulsation response. To evaluate chemical propulsion performance, NASA chemical equilibrium with applications calculations were performed at a chamber pressure of 300 psia and a nozzle expansion ratio of 50. HAN-rich mixtures showed higher adiabatic flame temperatures, increased specific impulse, and lower molecular-weight combustion products. Overall, the results demonstrate that mixtures containing 50%–75% HAN provide the most favorable balance between electrospray stability and combustion performance. This study identifies an optimal propellant composition range (50%–75% HAN) that simultaneously satisfies the competing demands of electrohydrodynamic emission stability and chemical propulsion performance, providing a key design guideline for future single-propellant hybrid propulsion systems.

results.title: Large droplet release
results.abstract: Abstract Large droplets, whose diameters exceed the capillary length, are inherently prone to instabilities during free fall due to capillary and inertial forces. We introduce an experimental platform that enables the controlled release of such drops while minimizing oscillatory breakup. By systematically varying surface curvature, porosity, and release acceleration, we identify the conditions under which droplet deformation is suppressed and near‐spherical integrity is maintained. High‐speed imaging reveals that curved, hydrophobic mesh surfaces with high porosity promote rapid detachment and attenuate elongation. In contrast, droplets released from solid substrates exhibit enhanced elongation and frequent fragmentation. The droplet aspect ratio at maximum stretch serves as a quantitative measure of stability across configurations. These findings advance the understanding of large droplet dynamics and provide experimentally validated guidelines for generating stable large droplets for applications involving fluid transport, atomization, and multiphase flow control.

results.title: Spontaneous Cyclic Levitation of Glycerol‐Water Droplets at Low Pressures
results.abstract: At low pressures, water often experiences chaotic multiphase transitions that complicate fluid management. Here, we demonstrate that a minimal addition of glycerol to a water droplet can transform these disruptive behaviors into highly regulated dynamics. Instead of typical breakup or rapid self-propulsion, freezing glycerol-water droplets enter a state of gentle, cyclic levitation, repeatedly undergoing "dwelling, liftoff, flight, and impact." We reveal that this phenomenon arises from the dual roles of glycerol. Freeze-concentration preserves interconnected liquid regions and prevents the formation of a closed outer ice shell, thereby limiting the accumulation of expansion-induced stress. In parallel, glycerol lowers the equilibrium freezing temperature, reducing the asymmetric vaporization recoil that drives self-propulsion during recalescence. The suppression of these instabilities enables a cyclic droplet motion driven by self-sustaining thermal oscillation, where basal heating enhances overpressure for liftoff and in-flight vaporization cooling resets the cycle. Our findings unveil a distinct regime of vaporization-driven droplet dynamics that is tunable through composition, offering new strategies for fluid management under extreme conditions, with implications ranging from thermal management to space exploration.

results.title: Genetic encoding and mutagenesis of RNA droplet phenotypes
results.abstract: RNA droplets assembled from cotranscriptionally folded nanostructures have recently emerged as a promising platform for constructing protocells and minimal synthetic cell models. A custom-designed DNA template encodes an RNA nanostar that self-assembles into droplets by kissing-loop interactions. Here we show that such RNA droplets encapsulate their DNA template, creating a genotype-phenotype link. We find that low mutation rates in the DNA template increase the phenotypical and functional complexity of the RNA droplets. Surprisingly, mutagenesis leads to the formation of long-lived vacuoles. With theory and next-generation sequencing, we explain this emergent behavior. We identify mutant nanostars that facilitate the formation of vacuoles through altered interactions between nanostars. Strikingly, vacuolated droplets exhibit micrometer-scale movement driven by internal vacuole dynamics - an emergent function resulting from mutagenesis. Beyond motility, we show that the vacuoles can be used as subcompartments to store cargo in the RNA droplets. Our findings establish RNA droplets as self-contained, evolvable systems, opening new avenues for the bottom-up evolution of synthetic cells and origins-of-life research.

results.title: Aero‐breakup of droplets: Recent progress and outlook
results.abstract: Abstract Aero‐breakup of droplets is a classic academic topic in fluid mechanics that describes the process of droplets breaking into multiple smaller ones or fine mists in an air flow. An in‐depth understanding of the aero‐breakup of liquid droplets is essential for the applications of spraying, atomization, ink printing, liquid fuel combustion, and other natural phenomenon explorations and industrial technology developments. Extensive studies have been conducted on this topic from different perspectives for decades. This review systematically summarizes the recent progress of droplet aero‐breakup studies. Starting from a brief introduction of research history, the intrinsic correlation between breakup modes and the governing parameters is sketched. The theoretical works on droplet breakup are first described from the views of interface instability theory and internal flow theory. These theories jointly construct the theoretical framework of droplet aero‐breakup. Second, several newly discovered breakup modes are demonstrated. Third, the influences of specific fluid properties, including viscosity, non‐Newtonian rheology, metallic natures, and volatility, on the mechanisms of droplet breakup are presented. The scenarios of multi‐droplet and droplet cloud are then discussed, which are believed to prevail in industrial applications. Last, an outlook for future explorations of droplet aero‐breakup is presented by providing several possible research directions.

results.title: Research progress and challenges of ionic wind propulsion for unmanned aerial vehicles
results.abstract: Abstract Since the maiden flight of the world’s first fixed-wing ionic wind-propelled unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) developed by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2018, ionic wind propulsion technology based on electrohydrodynamics has officially entered the stage of engineering exploration. Benefiting from no mechanical moving parts, low noise and rapid response, it has become a promising aerospace propulsion technology. This review illustrates the thrust generation mechanism of ionic wind, and summarizes recent advances in electrode structures, ducted thrusters, airborne power supplies, flight control and atmospheric factors, and further analyzes a series of engineering challenges and corresponding development strategies for ionic wind UAVs. This review is expected to provide a reference for subsequent research and practical applications of ionic wind propulsion for UAVs.

results.title: Sliding across veins becomes slipperier: Counterintuitive directional friction on nepenthes inner walls
results.abstract: Abstract Directional friction on soft interfaces combining wetting heterogeneity with compliant contact remains unclear under ultralow normal loads, where lubrication and contact geometry may interact strongly. We probed the inner wall of Nepenthes pitchers, which is naturally divided into a hydrophobic waxy zone and a hydrophilic digestive zone, by sliding a compliant sphere parallel and perpendicular to the venation under dry contact, water lubrication, and oil lubrication. Both zones consistently exhibited a counterintuitive frictional anisotropy, with higher average friction during venation-parallel sliding than during venation-perpendicular sliding. The waxy and digestive zones encoded this anisotropy primarily through directional roughness and wettability, respectively, supporting a groove–wetting–hydrodynamic framework for direction-dependent liquid-film load sharing and interfacial shear.

results.title: Worse urban environments increase transit use under peripheralization: Causal evidence from a natural experiment in Shanghai
Floquet mobility edges and transport in a periodically driven generalized Aubry-Andre model
results.abstract: We investigate the effect of a periodic electric field drive on the generalized Aubry-André model, also known as the Ganeshan-Pixley-Das Sarma (GPD) model, which is well known as a host of mobility edges. Our study of the Floquet spectrum of the driven GPD model uncovers the emergence of two distinct Floquet mobility edges, a delocalized--localized (DL) edge in the bounded regime, and a multifractal--localized (ML) edge in the unbounded regime. Using analytical results derived from Avila's global theory applied to the high frequency effective Hamiltonian, together with numerical diagnostics such as the fractal dimension and inverse participation ratio, we demonstrate that these mobility edges can be effectively controlled by the amplitude and frequency of the electric field drive. We also identify drive-induced localization at specific values of the driving parameters, corresponding to dynamical localization points in the absence of quasiperiodic potential. Furthermore, the dynamical study of the periodically driven GPD model demonstrates superdiffusive to almost ballistic transport in the bounded regime corresponding to the DL edges, whereas subdiffusive transport is observed in the unbounded regime associated with the ML edges. We also analyze deviations from the high-frequency effective description by explicitly examining the low-frequency driving regime, where significant and counterintuitive deviations in both spectral properties and transport behavior are observed. Our study highlights the interplay of a quasiperiodic potential and a periodically varying electric field drive as a powerful mechanism to engineer mobility edges and control transport in systems with rich spectral features.

results.title: The interplay between thermomigration and stress-driven hydrogen transport in metals
A Unified theory of transport barriers (TBs) in magnetically confined systems
results.abstract: Abstract A thermodynamic model of a plasma boundary layer, characterized by enhanced temperature contrasts is proposed. The theory is constructed to determine the inner boundary temperature T 1 for a specified outer (colder) boundary temperature T 0 , the heat flux F entering the inner boundary, and the parameters defining the layer. The system shows bifurcation and switches to a stable high gradient state if the heat flux F entering through the inner boundary exceeds a critical value F c . However there is an additional stringent condition for the transition to occur; the edge temperature T 0 must exceed a critical value T c -no transition is possible if T 0 < T c even for arbitrary large F . Equally important is the finding that F c is not a monotonic function of T 0 but has a minimum at T optimum ( = 4 T c ) in the model calculation. The confinement peaks at T optimum . The basic conceptual physics is obviously simple: The high contrast state becomes the preferred state when the incoming power into the layer is preferentially converted into coherent motions like the fluid flows and currents (undermining the standard diffusive processes that keep the lower temperature contrast). The purely macroscopic thermodynamic model bears excellent comparison with experimental and detailed microscopic inves

results.title: Nonreciprocal charge transport in quantum materials: From superconductors to magnetic systems
results.abstract: Nonreciprocal charge transport, where current flows preferentially in one direction, has become a key topic across quantum materials. This review covers some recent progress in bulk crystals, artificial heterostructures, van der Waals systems, high-temperature superconductors, and magnetic materials. The review discusses both intrinsic origins, such as band-structure effects, and extrinsic ones, including vortex motion, device geometry, and heating artifacts. A central focus is the superconducting diode effect due to its application potential, which shows different critical currents for opposite directions. The review also examines how symmetry breaking, spin-orbit coupling, and magnetic order contribute to the observed responses. However, there remain challenges when many exciting findings lack a unified picture, and the field continues to debate the relative importance of various mechanisms. The review highlights key open questions and suggests future directions, including better experimental standards and device integration. This review aims to give a balanced view of what is known, what is uncertain, and where the field might go next.

results.title: Evolutionary Mechanisms of Coagulation Factors in Cetaceans During Aquatic Adaptation
results.abstract: Cetaceans exhibit rapid wound healing in marine environments characterized by hypoxia and high pathogen loads, yet the adaptive mechanisms underlying their coagulation system remain poorly understood. We integrated evolutionary analyses with functional experiments to elucidate the molecular basis of specialized coagulation in cetaceans. Routine coagulation tests performed on Tursiops truncatus (n = 3) and Bos taurus (n = 3) showed that T. truncatus plasma exhibited significantly shortened prothrombin time and thrombin time, as well as prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT). Evolutionary analyses revealed that 18 genes were under positive selection in cetaceans, with F11 showing accelerated evolution and lineage-specific amino acid substitutions. APTT mixing assays showed that bovine plasma shortened the prolonged APTT of T. truncatus plasma, suggesting that differences in intrinsic pathway components may contribute to the cetacean coagulation phenotype. Compared to B. taurus, Tursiops truncatus coagulation factor VII increased protein abundance, while factor V abundance was reduced. Plasma proteomic analysis further suggested that differentially expressed proteins were enriched in pathways related to lipid metabolism, the coagulation cascade, and antiviral responses. In conclusion, the cetacean coagulation system has undergone adaptive evolution at both genetic and protein levels. Key amino acid changes such as coagulation factor XI (FXI) and coagulation factor VII (FVII) may optimize coagulation balance by modulating protein interaction strengths; the conserved evolution and increased plasma abundance of PLG may indicate a potential contribution of fibrinolytic regulation to cetacean coagulation balance. This study provides coagulation biology evidence for physiological adaptation in aquatic mammals.

results.title: Golgi-Associated ATG8ylation: Mechanisms and Biological Implications
results.abstract: ATG8ylation, the covalent conjugation of LC3/GABARAP-family proteins to lipids or proteins, is no longer viewed solely as a signature of canonical degradative autophagy. A rapidly growing literature has revealed that ATG8 conjugation also occurs on pre-existing single membranes through noncanonical autophagy, a process also referred to as conjugation of ATG8 to single membranes (CASM). The Golgi apparatus has emerged as a particularly important and conceptually revealing platform for this biological process. Recent studies have established that Golgi-associated ATG8ylation is not a passive by-product of organelle disruption, but a regulated response that can be initiated at the Golgi, often depends on the V-ATPase-ATG16L1 machinery, promotes stress-responsive transcriptional programs involving TFE3 and TFEB, mediates unconventional secretion of IL1β, and supports the repair of damaged Golgi architecture. Here, we synthesize these advances into a unified model in which Golgi-associated ATG8ylation functions as a membrane stress-response hub. In this model, Golgi perturbations are sensed through local changes in organelle state, including trafficking blockade, pH/ion imbalance, V-ATPase assembly, and cytoskeletal or ribbon disruption. These signals recruit or activate ATG8 conjugation machinery on Golgi membranes and generate functional outputs: membrane remodeling, Golgi repair, transcriptional stress adaptation, and unconventional secretion. We also discuss unresolved questions concerning membrane specificity, lipid acceptors, the distinction between repair and degradation, and the physiological roles of this pathway.

results.title: Niche Occupation and Rapid Adaptation Mechanisms of Invasive Guppies in Polluted Water Bodies
results.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems are facing a global biodiversity crisis and biological invasion crisis at the same time. The guppy (Poecilia reticulata) is one of the most invasive fish species worldwide. It can successfully live in polluted water, providing a good model for studying eco-evolutionary processes of rapid adaptation and ecological niche occupation. This paper reviews the progress of ecological niche occupation and rapid adaptation mechanisms of invasive guppies in polluted waters. Existing research shows that the guppy can have its native range from South America to almost 70 countries in the world, and it often affects native species, such as resource competition, reproductive interference and changes in ecological functions. A polluted environment is conducive to rapid adaptation of guppy with multi-level, including life-history characteristics (transformation to an r-selection strategy), sexually selected characteristics (change and microevolution of sexually selected characteristics such as ornamental colors), the molecular-level variation or response (for example, CYP1A gene selection, transcriptome changes).On the other hand, the rapid adaptation of guppies, in turn, favours their niche occupation, giving rise to a positive feedback loop of "pollution→adaptation→invasion persistence". Currently, this field still has deficiencies in the balance of geographic coverage and the degree of contributions from phenotypic plasticity and genetic adaptation. This paper suggests that future studies should strengthen the cross-regional comparison and utilize genomic methods to integrate with field ecological observations to provide a scientific basis for the governance of invasion of polluted waters.

results.title: Physiological mechanisms of drought and high temperature adaptation in Lens species: A review
results.abstract: Abstract Lentil ( Lens culinaris Medik.) is an important grain legume known for its nutritional quality, agronomic value, and role in sustainable agriculture. However, its genetic diversity is limited due to domestication, constraining efforts to breed stress‐resilient cultivars, especially under climate change. Crop wild relatives (CWRs) represent a valuable source of untapped genetic variability, harboring adaptive traits shaped under extreme environments. This review emphasizes the potential of CWRs in lentil breeding for abiotic stress tolerance, particularly drought and heat stress. It explores key abiotic stresses impacting lentil productivity, discusses mechanisms of stress tolerance available in wild lentil species, and highlights the necessity to integrate these traits into modern breeding programs. Utilizing the genetic diversity in CWRs can overcome current breeding limitations, improve lentil resilience, and secure sustainable production amid growing environmental challenges.

results.title: Inferring Adaptation at Community Composition Level From the Relationship Between Succession Rate and Global Change Intensity
results.abstract: ABSTRACT In response to anthropogenic environmental changes, biological communities often undergo compositional changes, which are traditionally thought to represent adaptation. However, this hypothesis and its mechanism remain surprisingly underexplored. In this study, we conducted a 10‐year nitrogen deposition experiment in the Eurasian steppe, manipulating nine intensities under two management strategies (fencing or mowing). As the intensity increased from 0–20 to 50 g N m −2 yr −1 , the succession rates of both plant and soil microbial communities first increased but then decreased, implying that high intensities of N deposition exceed the capacity of community adaptation. In addition, both the succession rate of the deterministic component of community compositional variation and the succession rate of soil physicochemical characteristics increased and then decreased with increasing N intensity. They were positively correlated, demonstrating that adaptation is primarily driven by deterministic ecological processes. Meanwhile, mowing promoted the plant community's adaptation, while fencing promoted adaptation of the microbial community, both by restraining stochastic processes. Overall, to enable biological communities to adapt compositionally to environmental changes, we should aim to limit the intensity of changes below certain thresholds, and implement reasonable strategies, whether deterministic (e.g., restoring soil physicochemical conditions) or stochastic (e.g., adding seeds of adaptive species).

results.title: Climate Change and Soil Health in Agroecosystems: A Review of Feedback Mechanisms, Vulnerabilities, and Adaptation Strategies
results.abstract: Climate change is increasingly affecting soil health in agroecosystems through changes in temperature, precipitation, atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations, and the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events. Soil health, which encompasses physical structure, chemical fertility, biological activity, and the capacity to sustain ecosystem functions, plays a critical role in agricultural productivity, climate regulation, water conservation, and food security. This review examines the interactions between climate change and soil health, emphasizing feedback mechanisms, vulnerabilities across agroecosystems, and adaptation strategies for enhancing agricultural resilience. The review synthesizes established scientific literature on soil organic carbon dynamics, greenhouse gas emissions, soil moisture regulation, erosion, nutrient cycling, microbial communities, and soil biodiversity. The evidence indicates that warming can accelerate soil organic matter decomposition and nutrient mineralization, while droughts and intense rainfall can increase erosion, disrupt microbial processes, and reduce nutrient retention. Conversely, healthy soils with high organic matter content, stable aggregates, diverse microbial communities, and effective water infiltration can contribute to climate mitigation and improve resilience to climatic extremes. However, these benefits depend on soil type, climate, land management, and the availability of water and nutrients. Adaptation approaches, including conservation agriculture, cover cropping, diversified crop rotations, organic amendments, agroforestry, improved nutrient management, and integrated soil and water conservation, can help maintain soil functionality under changing climatic conditions. Their effectiveness varies according to local environmental and socioeconomic circumstances, and some interventions involve trade-offs related to greenhouse gas emissions, water use, and implementation costs. The review concludes that protecting soil health requires integrated, locally appropriate management supported by long-term monitoring, farmer participation, and policies that recognize soils as both vulnerable resources and essential components of climate adaptation and mitigation.
